name: Rosemary
description: An evergreen woody perennial with needle-like leaves and pine-like fragrance. Essential for roasting meats and root vegetables.

growingConditions.watering: Allow soil to dry out between waterings

uses: Infused in artisan breads like focaccia

video.title: Rosemary Growing Guide: Planting, Growing & Propagation

uses: Rosemary tea traditionally used to aid digestion and ease headaches
Aroma associated in folk use with alertness and memory
Infused oil massaged into muscles for aches and stiffness
benefits: High in antioxidants, including rosmarinic and carnosic acid
Has natural antimicrobial properties that help preserve food
May support circulation and reduce minor inflammation
medicinal.caution: Rosemary in medicinal amounts is not recommended during pregnancy. Cooking amounts are generally safe.

taste: Piney, woody and slightly peppery, with a lemony hint.
sideEffects: Large medicinal amounts can upset the stomach
Rosemary oil can irritate the skin
May raise blood pressure in sensitive people when taken in large amounts

safety.allergy: Rosemary is a mint-family plant, so allergic reactions are possible in people sensitive to it. Rosemary oil can cause skin rashes.
safety.pregnancy: Cooking amounts are fine, but medicinal amounts are not recommended during pregnancy.
safety.pets: Rosemary is generally regarded as non-toxic to cats and dogs in small amounts, but the essential oil is not safe for them.
safety.medications: Large amounts may affect blood thinners, blood pressure medicines and some other drugs. Ask your doctor if you take them.

temperature: Likes warmth and sun, at about 15-30 °C. Many types survive about -10 °C, but a hard frost can kill it, so protect it or bring pots inside.
harvest: Snip 5-8 cm tips of fresh, soft growth at any time of year. Never take more than a third of the plant at once, and do not cut into bare woody stems, because they rarely regrow.
storage: Wrap fresh sprigs in a damp paper towel in the fridge for up to two weeks. Rosemary dries very well when hung in bunches, and sprigs can be frozen whole.
dailyLife: Roast with potatoes, chicken, lamb or vegetables
Stir into bread dough or olive oil
Use woody stems as skewers for grilling
Brew a sprig in hot water for an aromatic tea
tips: Water only when the soil is dry, as too much water causes root rot
Grow it by a sunny wall for shelter
Bring potted plants indoors in cold climates

origin.details: Rosemary grows wild on the dry, sunny hills along the Mediterranean coast. Its Latin name means dew of the sea.
